bio.en: Adam Fishman is a veteran growth and product leader who was Lyft's first growth hire, later led product and growth at Patreon where he helped build one of the most successful creator platforms, and today advises companies and teaches growth through his newsletter and Reforge.
bio.zh: Adam Fishman 是一位资深的增长与产品领导者，曾是 Lyft 最早的 growth 招聘员工，后来在 Patreon 主导产品与增长、参与打造业内最成功的创作者平台之一，如今通过他的 Newsletter 和 Reforge 为企业做顾问并教授增长。

summary.en: Adam lays out his Growth Competency Model with four pillars—growth execution, customer knowledge, growth strategy, and communication & influence—arguing the goal is to build a balanced team, not hire a mythical 11-out-of-10 unicorn. He makes the case that onboarding is the most underrated growth lever because it touches 100% of users and drives retention; at Patreon, connecting creators with the right person at the right time and then productizing that lifted creator revenue by 25%. On hiring, he favors internal transfers or rising talent strong on execution and customer knowledge, bringing in specialists like SEO only once the fundamentals are in place. Finally, his PMF framework (People, Mission, Financials) helps candidates evaluate employers—do backchannel references and observe exec-team dynamics before you commit.
summary.zh: Adam 提出了「增长能力模型」，包含四大支柱——增长执行、客户认知、增长战略、沟通与影响力——目的是组建能力互补的均衡团队，而不是去寻找一个样样 11 分的独角兽。他把引导流程（onboarding）视为最被低估的增长杠杆：它触达 100% 的用户、塑造第一印象，并直接驱动留存；在 Patreon，通过在对的时间把创作者连到真人、再把这些做法产品化，把创作者的前两个月收入提升了 25%。招聘上他建议优先内部转岗或上升期人才（看重执行力和客户认知），只有在基础打牢后才从外部引入 SEO 之类的专家。最后他用「PMF 框架」（人 People、使命 Mission、财务 Financials）帮求职者评估雇主，主张做反向背景调查、观察高管团队的互动动态，再决定要不要加入。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Onboarding is the only part of your product experience that a hundred percent of people are ever going to touch. Good luck getting a hundred percent feature adoption of anything else in your product, right? But onboarding is the thing that you have to go through in order to use the product. It's also the first opportunity that you have as a company to deliver on the promise that you made out in the marketplace. So I like to think of your brand is the promise that you're making and your product experience is your delivery of that promise. And those two things have to be in lockstep with each other, or you're going to have mismatched expectations and some really disappointed customers. So this is the first chance that a customer has to be really excited or really disappointed in what they thought they were getting. So don't mess that up.
turns.zh: 引导流程（onboarding）是你产品体验里唯一一个百分之百的用户都会触碰到的部分。你想让产品里其他任何功能的采用率达到百分之百？祝你好运，对吧？但引导流程是用户为了用你的产品必须经过的一关。而且，这也是你作为一家公司，第一次有机会去兑现你在市场上做出的承诺。所以我喜欢这么想：你的品牌就是你做出的承诺，而你的产品体验就是你兑现承诺的方式。这两件事必须步调一致，否则用户的期待就会错位，然后你就会收获一批大失所望的客户。这是客户第一次有机会对自己以为能得到的产品感到兴奋或者失望。所以千万别搞砸了。

turns.zh: 我一开始就特想问一个问题：你在 Lyft 去得非常早。我猜那是一段特别疯狂的旅程。我很好奇，你在 Lyft 那段时光里最具体的记忆是什么？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: I have a ton of memories from the almost three years that I was there, but I think the biggest one, and probably the most tactile or memorable thing was when we launched Lyft, when we were bringing it out of private beta, we had this press event at the office, which is in Soma, and it had these doors, these big huge garage style doors. And so we opened them up and we actually drove a car into the office with a pink mustache on the front of it, and then a bunch of drivers piled out of it and met the press members and were high fiving people and stuff like that. And then we also served a giant pink mustache cake at this event. So of all of the things there, that one sticks in my head the most.
turns.zh: 在那将近三年里我有很多回忆，但最大、也最有画面感、最难忘的，应该是我们让 Lyft 走出私测、正式上线的时候。我们在办公室搞了一个媒体发布会，办公室在 Soma 区，有一扇很大的车库式大门。我们把门打开，真的开了一辆前面挂着粉色大胡子的车进办公室，然后一堆司机从车上下来，跟媒体见面、击掌什么的。我们还在一个活动上摆了一个巨大的粉色胡子蛋糕。所以在所有事情里，这一幕在我脑子里最深刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I hope there was no hair in this mustache cake.
turns.zh: 太喜欢了。我希望这个胡子蛋糕里没有头发。

turns.en: No, no, there was not. It was delicious.
turns.zh: 没有，没有，很好吃。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yeah, I have seen it. I actually read the book first. I've been a pretty big fan of Mike Isaac, who's the New York Times reporter who wrote it. It was like renavigating, relitigating a history that I had lived through already. And so much of that story was stuff that I had experienced pretty regularly while I was at Lyft battling against Uber.
turns.zh: 对，我看过了。其实我先读了原书。我一直挺喜欢 Mike Isaac，就是写这本书的纽约时报记者。所以我长期都很关注他的报道。他写书的时候我跟他有过一些交流。我觉得里面有些部分挺痛苦的，就像重新走一遍、重新审判一段我已经活过的历史。而且那个故事里很多事，都是我在 Lyft 跟 Uber 打仗的时候经常经历的。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: So one part of me was like, "I remember that. God, that was hard." Another part of me was happy to see that all of the things were out in the open finally, things that were hard to talk about about competitive practices and stuff like that and just shady things. And some part of me was happy that it was out there. And then one other thing separately, so I actually was interviewing with Joseph Gordon-Levitt to be an advisor with his company HitRecord while he was filming Super Bumped.
turns.zh: 所以我一方面会觉得「我记得那个，天，那真难」。另一方面我又很高兴终于把那些事摊开在阳光下——那些关于不正当竞争手段、那些见不得光的事，之前很难开口谈。所以某部分的我挺开心它终于被公之于众。还有一件单独的事：其实我当时正在跟 Joseph Gordon-Levitt 面试，想当他公司 HitRecord 的顾问，那时他正在拍《Super Pumped》。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And we had this conversation over Zoom when he was on break in between scenes of filming the show. And for those who don't know, he's the guy that plays Travis Kalanick, the CEO and founder of Uber. So he did this interview with me and he was in his trailer on set, fully decked out as TK in his look with his hair slicked back. And it was really funny and also cool to see him in this context. And he is probably the polar opposite from Travis Kalanick. Obviously they're both super successful, but JGL is a really down to earth, nice, very family-oriented calm guy. So anyways, this is a funny story of my time meeting and interviewing with him.
turns.zh: 我们是在 Zoom 上聊的，当时他正夹在拍戏的间隙。不了解的人可能不知道，他就是演 Travis Kalanick——Uber 的 CEO 兼创始人——的那个人。所以他来面试我的时候，是在片场的拖车里，全套 TK 造型，头发往后梳，扮相齐全。看到他在那个场景里特别好笑，也很酷。而且他大概跟 Travis Kalanick 完全相反。当然两人都很成功，但 JGL 是个特别接地气、人很好、很顾家、很平静的人。总之，这是我跟他面试见面的一段趣事。

turns.zh: 好，很期待听这些。我们前面简单提过，你最近写了更多东西。你有 fishmanafnewsletter.com 这个 Newsletter，最近还写了一篇超硬核的文章叫《增长能力模型》，基本就是讲招增长负责人要看什么、怎么招、怎么评估、该把技能重点放在哪之类的。第一个问题：你为什么觉得非写这篇不可？你发现创始人在招和评估增长负责人时常犯什么错？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yeah, so first I'm going to put up my new background here, which is my growth competency model background. For those watching on YouTube, I have a funny graphic in the background for this. So I guess the reason that I wrote this, there were a few reasons that I wrote it. One is it really felt necessary to write it. And at first it's, I don't think I've ever come across this type of canonical reference before around how to hire and plan for growth. So that's number one. I didn't think it existed. It needed to exist.
turns.zh: 对，首先我把这个新背景图放上，就是我的增长能力模型背景图。在 YouTube 上看的朋友，我背后放了张搞笑的图。我写这篇的原因有几个。一是真的觉得有必要写。一开始是觉得，我好像从没见过这种关于怎么招人、怎么规划增长的权威参考。所以第一，我觉得它不存在，它需要存在。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Two, as an advisor and someone who has held the head of growth role many times, I get asked this question a lot. I get asked all the time about how do you hire growth people? And it's usually something like, "Hey, how do we find you but 10 years earlier in your career?" And it feels like that question is missing the first principles approach to hiring a growth person. And if you're doing that, you're just pattern matching to me. And I may not be the best person, right, or somebody who looks like me may not be the best person. So I think we're missing that.
turns.zh: 第二，作为顾问、而且多次当过增长负责人的人，我老被问这个问题。大家总问我「怎么招增长的人？」通常都是「嘿，怎么找到十年前的你？」这种问法。但我觉得这个问题缺了招增长人才的第一性原理思路。如果只这么问，你就是在拿我来套模板。而我未必是最合适的人，对吧，或者长得像我的人也未必最合适。所以这块是缺的。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And then third, one of the programs that I'm currently creating is around growth leadership. And so I've been thinking a lot about what it takes to be an exceptional growth leader, how you hire other people onto your team and create balanced teams. And this is going to be a really important component of that program. So it was just really top of mind. So yeah, that's why I wrote it.
turns.zh: 第三，我现在在做的项目里有一个是关于增长领导的。所以我一直在想，要成为一个出色的增长领导者需要什么、怎么招人到团队里、怎么组建均衡的团队。这会是我那个项目里非常重要的一部分。所以那阵子它就在我最脑子里转。所以，这就是我写它的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me ask one quick question and I think you were about to start answering one mistakes founders make, but I guess it's less of a question. I know this was built on another model for product management, which is really awesome. And I love that there's this growing fountain of career ladders, competencies per function. And so I don't know if there's been one that's really great for design and engineering, but I love that this is happening. And so first of all, I just want to say I appreciate that you put in the time to think this through.
turns.zh: 我快速插个问题，我想你正要开始讲创始人犯的错，不过我倒觉得这不是个问题。我知道这个模型是建立在另一个产品经理模型之上的，特别赞。而且我很喜欢现在这种按职能细分的职业阶梯、能力模型越来越多地涌现。我不知道设计和工程有没有特别好的，但我喜欢这种趋势。所以首先，我只是想说，我很感激你花时间把这件事想透。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Cool. Thank you. Yeah, and I do think we need more of these. I think we need one for marketers, I think we need one for engineers, designers, research probably, there's probably a bunch of functions that could benefit from some canonicalized resource around this stuff. So yeah, some myths and mistakes that I think founders made and that I've made. I've definitely lived through some mistakes. A few experiences where I was hired into a company where the founder had really messed up expectations of what a growth person should be doing, what I should be doing. And I wanted to set the record straight for founders because they are the folks who hire for this and other leaders.
turns.zh: 酷，谢谢。对，我也觉得我们需要更多这种东西。市场人员需要，工程师、设计师、研究员大概也需要，很多职能都能从这种权威资源里受益。所以，说说我认为是创始人、也是我本人犯过的一些误区吧。我确实踩过一些坑。有几次我被招进一家公司，创始人对于增长的人该干啥、我该干啥，期待完全错位。我想帮创始人澄清一下，因为招人的就是他们，还有其他领导。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: So one example that comes to mind is, I did a very brief stint at a company called Wyzant, in between Lyft and Patreon. And the founders of that company, so Wyzant was a tutoring marketplace. It was acquired by a company not too long ago, so it's now part of a bigger learning company. And the founders of that company we're looking for what I would call a silver bullet strategy to their growth challenges. And what they really needed, and I was naive and didn't think about asking these questions or about evaluating this properly, what they really needed was to create a strategy to add on new growth loops and a system for how to execute against that strategy.
turns.zh: 想到一个例子：在 Lyft 和 Patreon 之间，我在一家叫 Wyzant 的公司短暂待过。Wyzant 是个家教撮合平台，不久前被收购了，现在属于一个更大的教育公司。那家公司的创始人想要的，是我所谓的「银弹战略」来解决增长问题。但他们真正需要的——我当时太天真，没想着问这些问题、也没好好评估——其实是建立一套增长闭环的战略，以及一个执行这套战略的系统。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: If we had talked about that as part of evaluating each other, as part of them evaluating me, it would've given me a lot of confidence that it was the right hire to make. But the problem was they didn't approach it that way. They didn't ask me those questions and I was too naive to recognize that, "Hey, they're not actually evaluating this with the competencies that you would expect for a growth leader." Executing a growth strategy takes time and patience, and they didn't really have it. And overall it ended rather unsuccessfully. I helped them build this office in San Francisco, hired a bunch of folks, we actually closed down the office. I had to lay off a bunch of the people that I'd hired, including myself, which wasn't particularly fun. And I think all of it comes back to that they didn't have a really strong set of criteria on what it meant to hire a great growth person. And so if I can help even just a little bit with founders making that decision better, it'll lead to fewer mismatches I think in the hiring process.
turns.zh: 如果我们当时在互相评估的时候聊过这些，作为他们评估我的一部分，我会更有信心这是个对的招聘。但问题是他们没那么做。他们没问我那些问题，我也太天真，没意识到「嘿，他们其实没在用增长负责人该有的能力来评估」。执行增长战略需要时间和耐心，而他们真的没有。最后整体挺失败的。我帮他们在旧金山建了个办公室，招了一堆人，结果办公室关了。我不得不把我招的人——包括我自己——都裁掉，那可不好玩。而这一切都回到一点：他们对「招一个好增长人」没有一套很强的标准。所以哪怕只是帮创始人把这个决定做得好一点，我觉得也能少一些招聘中的错配。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Let's get into it. What are the components of this model? And you can put it back up again for folks to follow along in the background.
turns.zh: 太棒了。来，进入正题。这个模型有哪些组成部分？你可以再把它放出来，方便大家跟着看背景。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: It's coming back.
turns.zh: 回来了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like a TikTok.
turns.zh: 像 TikTok 一样。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: The whole thing looks like a big circle and there's four wedges in that circle, four equal parts. And I think that answer of what are the components, what should people look for, really, I'll give the PM answer, which is it depends. And what does it depend on? It depends on the state of the team and where the skill gaps are. So the goal of the competency model is not to find a unicorn human being that is an 11 out of 10 on every one of these things, because frankly, that person doesn't exist. I am not an 11 out of 10 on these skills and I have been a growth executive at many companies. I consider myself to be pretty good at the job. The goal is to create a well-rounded team so that you're hiring and balancing skills across your team and that you don't have any gaps in your portfolio.
turns.zh: 整体看起来是个大圆圈，圈里有四个扇形，四等份。至于「有哪些组成部分、该看什么」，我会给一个产品经理式的回答：看情况。看什么情况？看团队的状态和技能缺口在哪。所以这个能力模型的目的，不是找一个在每一样上都 11 分（满分 10 分）的独角兽人类，因为说实话这种人不存在。我在好几家公司当过增长高管，我在这些技能上也不是 11 分，但我自认干得相当不错。目标是组建一个均衡的团队，让技能在团队里互补，组合里不留缺口。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And so when you think about it, there are four main components to the growth competency model. And the four big components or buckets are growth execution, customer knowledge, growth strategy, and then the last one is communication and influence. And each of those has three really specific skills. And so to give an example, let's break down growth execution for example, which is one of the very first ones that you should be good at if you're a growth practitioner. Within this competency grouping, there's three individual competencies that are channel fluency, experimentation, and what I'd call productizing learnings. And so you can evaluate and ask questions to understand how good people are at these different things and what their experience has been with them.
turns.zh: 所以拆开看，增长能力模型有四个主要部分，四个大块：增长执行、客户认知、增长战略，最后一个就是沟通与影响力。每一块又包含三个非常具体的技能。举个例子，比如「增长执行」，这是你做增长的首先得擅长的。这一组里又有三个单项能力：渠道熟练度、实验能力，还有我所说的「把经验产品化」。你可以问问题、做评估，来了解一个人在这些方面有多强、有什么经验。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: So in productizing learnings for example, one of the key things that a growth person has to do is generate hypotheses, learn from those hypotheses and then translate that into changes that they're making in the product. And you want to find somebody who has a track record of at least understanding how to take something they have learned that might be an experiment or something that's very NVP and turn that into something that has hooks into different areas of the product. And so that's a critical skill to evaluate. And one of an example, the overall set of competencies.
turns.zh: 比如在「把经验产品化」里，增长的人必须做的一件关键事是：提出假设、从假设里学习，然后把这些转化成产品里的改动。你要找的是那种至少有能力把学到的东西——可能是一个实验，或者某个很 MVP 的东西——变成能挂到产品各个角落的钩子的人。所以这是要评估的关键技能，也是整体能力的一个例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To throw in a question real quick, is one way to use this model, coming back to your Wyzant example where there's of course misalignment between you and the founder to sit down and look at this circle here and be like, "Here's where I'm strong, here's where maybe we need to hire someone to take over."
turns.zh: 快速插个问题：用这个模型的一个方式，回到你 Wyzant 的例子——你和创始人之间明显错位——就是坐下来看这个圆圈，然后说「这是我强的地方，这是可能需要招个人来接手的地方」？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. You can almost use it as a reverse interviewing characteristic and say, "What are the competencies you, founder, CEO, care about? What's really important to you for the first person in this role? Or the expectations that you have of what I will bring to the table." And then you can be really candid about what you're good at and what you're not good at, where you're developing. So yeah, I agree with that for sure.
turns.zh: 对，绝对可以。你几乎可以把它当成一个反向面试的工具，问「创始人、CEO，你最看重哪些能力？招第一个人进来，你最在意什么？或者你对我要带来的东西有什么期待？」然后你可以很坦诚地说自己擅长什么、不擅长什么、在哪些地方还在成长。所以我完全同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I know this also plays into evaluating your performance and it could be like, "Hey Adam, here's the three things that we want to focus on in the next cycle."
turns.zh: 太棒了。我知道这也能用来评估你的表现，比如「嘿 Adam，这是下个周期我们要聚焦的三件事」。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: For sure. Yeah. It's really a good foundational framework for being really concrete and specific in the feedback that you provide someone. So rather than saying, "Adam, you really need to be more strategic." Everybody's heard that at some point and it's like, "Well, what do you mean?" You can say, "Hey, we need to work on the area of growth strategy and that means I need to see better modeling of loops out of you, better understanding communication of what those loops are." And you can give really concrete feedback.
turns.zh: 当然。对。它确实是一个很好的基础框架，能让你的反馈非常具体。与其说「Adam，你得更有战略眼光」，大家都听过这种话，然后心想「你到底什么意思？」你可以说「嘿，我们需要在增长战略这块下功夫，意思是我要看到你把闭环建模得更好，更清楚地沟通这些闭环是什么」。这样反馈就非常具体。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So we've talked about growth execution, What's next?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们聊了增长执行，接下来呢？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: The next one is what I would call customer knowledge. And within customer knowledge there's a set of things and really this is about data fluency and instrumentation, understanding user psychology, which is a big one, and then this idea of being able to experiment and learn over time and how you develop your narrative and your creative approach to talking to customers. I love user psychology and it's one of the things that I think attracted me to growth and to product. I studied consumer psychology when I was in college and I'm just probably would've been a psychologist if not for a growth practitioner, which is a weird other approach I could have taken in my career. But-
turns.zh: 下一个是我所谓的「客户认知」。客户认知里有一组东西，核心是关于数据熟练度和埋点、理解用户心理（这块很大），还有这个随着时间实验和学习的想法，以及你怎么发展出跟客户沟通的话术和创意方式。我超爱用户心理，这也是当初吸引我进入增长和产品的原因。我大学学的是消费心理学，要不是做了增长，我大概会是个心理学家——那是另一种可能的人生路径。不过——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's not too late to pivot.
turns.zh: 现在转行也不晚。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: ... Second career. Yeah, actually, announcing today I'm pivoting the newsletter to just talk about therapy and psychology.
turns.zh: ……第二职业。对，其实今天宣布一下，我要把 Newsletter 转型，专门聊疗愈和心理学。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes. This is going to be the title of the podcast.
turns.zh: 好。这就是这期播客的标题。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Awesome. So like user psychology, I think one of the things that people don't easily understand is that most people come to your product with an emotional frame and a lot of people want to appeal to their logical brain right away. And the reality is, don't do that. And so you have to understand the mindset that people are in. How low are their lows? How high are their highs? Why are they seeking out your product? And it often, as I mentioned, stems from some emotional challenge that they're having or something that they're seeking. And it's not because your product is the best chat bot or because it gives the best answers. There's a different thing that they're trying to solve. And only when you address that can you move on to those other things. So that's the second competency is, customer knowledge.
turns.zh: 太棒了。说到用户心理，我觉得很多人不容易理解的一点是：大多数人带着情绪框架来用你的产品，而很多人一上来就想打动他们的逻辑脑。现实是，别那么做。你得理解用户处在什么心态。他们的低谷有多低？高峰有多高？他们为什么来找你的产品？而且往往就像我说的，源于他们正经历某种情绪上的挑战，或者他们在寻求某种东西。不是因为你产品是最好的聊天机器人，或者能给出最好的答案。他们想解决的是另一回事。只有你先解决那个，才能接着谈别的。所以这是第二个能力：客户认知。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me of something I mentioned on some podcast recently, this tweet that one of the Collison brothers tweeted about how user research is often misunderstood in that people think you do user research and that informs what you build. And instead the way you think about it is user research informs your model of your customer and that model informs what you build.
turns.zh: 这让我想起我最近在别的播客上提到过的一件事——Collison 兄弟里有一位发过一条推文，说用户研究经常被误解：人们以为做用户研究是为了指导你该造什么。但其实正确的做法是，用户研究是在完善你对客户的「模型」，而这个模型再去指导你该造什么。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the more user research you do, the more your model evolves to help you understand the customer. And that's been really helpful for me because I never thought of it that way.
turns.zh: 你做的用户研究越多，这个模型就越演化，越能帮你理解客户。这对我特别有帮助，因为我以前从没这么想过。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yeah. I think that's a great example. Seeking the solution in a customer interview is never going to work, right? You seek to understand and then you take that away and you can think through what the model should look like and how things should change as a result. Yeah. That's great. I can cover the third and fourth competency-
turns.zh: 对，我觉得这是个很好的例子。在客户访谈里直接找解决方案，永远行不通，对吧？你是为了理解，然后把理解带走，再去想那个模型应该长什么样、该相应做哪些改变。对。这个我接着讲第三和第四项能力——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's good.
turns.zh: 很好。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: ... and I'll try to be a little more brief on that.
turns.zh: ……我会尽量讲得简短点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, no. It's good.
turns.zh: 不，不，挺好的。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: The third competency is growth strategy. And now the third and fourth competencies I would say are a bit more advanced topics. And again, remember when I said people index higher or lower on these as they go across their career, I would expect a more junior growth person to not necessarily be a 10 out of 10 on strategy and communication. These are things that you really have to work at a long time. They tend to be softer skills in a lot of cases and you learn best by either getting it very right or getting it very wrong. And so you've got to put in the time to develop these. But in growth strategy, there's three. The first one is growth loop modeling. So really understanding how you grow and where you should be spending your time. What acquires users? What retains them? What monetizes them?
turns.zh: 第三项是增长战略。我想说，第三和第四项能力是稍微进阶一点的话题。再说一遍我前面讲的：人在职业生涯不同阶段，在这些能力上高低不同。我会预期一个比较初级的增长人员，在战略和沟通上未必是 10 分。这些是真得长期磨练的。很多情况下它们偏软技能，最好的学习方式要么是大获成功、要么是大栽跟头。所以你得花时间培养。增长战略里有三块。第一是增长闭环建模。也就是真正理解你是怎么增长的、时间该花在哪。什么带来用户？什么留住他们？什么让他们付费？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: The second one is capital allocation and forecasting. This is basically where are you deploying either your money, your people, how are you managing the portfolio and how are you projecting that out into the future? And that's a really hard one. You have to become best buddies with your finance friends in order to do that. And so anyways, that's capital allocation and forecasting. And then the third one is prioritization and road mapping. So you have to be able to sequence the work much like in building a product, right? Building your growth strategy, you have to sequence it. That sequence has to make sense based on your growth models. You have to have the capital or the people to allocate to that stuff. And you have to be able to build a series of hypotheses in a series of solutions to test against those hypotheses so that you can learn and then productize to those learnings.
turns.zh: 第二是资本配置和预测。基本就是你要往哪投钱、投人，你怎么管理这个组合、怎么把它投射到未来？这个很难。你得跟财务的哥们儿变成好哥们才能做好。总之这就是资本配置和预测。第三是优先级排序和路线图。你得像做产品一样给工作排序，对吧？搭建增长战略，你得排好顺序。这个顺序得跟你的增长模型对得上。你得有资金或人力去配给这些东西。而且你得能围绕假设，构建一系列假设和解决方案去测试，这样你才能学，再把学到的东西产品化。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And there's a lot of ways to test this stuff. Situational, behavioral, interviewing, I talk a lot about this in my post on hiring growth. There's like very specific questions you can ask to understand what people have done or what they might do in different situations. There's case studies and things like that. So that's the third one. And then the fourth one is communication and influence.
turns.zh: 测试这些有很多方法。情境式的、行为式的、面试式的，我在那篇讲招聘增长的文章里讲了很多。有非常具体的问题，能帮你了解一个人做过什么、在不同情境下会怎么做。还有案例分析之类的。所以这是第三项。第四项是沟通与影响力。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And I would say, I think you probably know this as a PM, influence is one of the biggest and hardest skills to develop. It's no different in a growth practitioner and in some cases it can even be harder because sometimes people come in with a preconceived notion of what growth is and isn't and you have to change their mind. And so within communication and influence, there's strategic communication. So how do a series of experiments and a series of things that you're trying, fit into the overall picture of a bigger bet that you're taking?
turns.zh: 我想说，你作为 PM 大概也知道，影响力是最重要、也最难培养的能力之一。对增长从业者也不例外，有些情况下甚至更难，因为有时候人们对「增长是什么、不是什么」有先入为主的观念，你得改变他们的想法。在沟通与影响力里，第一是战略沟通。也就是你做的一系列实验、一系列尝试，怎么放进你正在下的一盘大棋的整体图景里？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: How do you lead a team? So team leadership is a big part of communication and influence. And then how do you manage stakeholders? And this is hard in growth because often growth can be viewed as at odds with really thoughtful and quality craftsmanship and product building, but it's not. Those things go hand in hand. And so you really have to win people over on what it means to do growth. And I would say, this is the pinnacle, right? This is the hardest one. It's a lifelong journey. It relies very extensively on understanding people and who you're talking to. And those people can be very different from company to company and the currency that they trade in can be really different. And so this one is one where you have to go back to square one and relearn who the people are that you're working with every time you step into a new role or a new company or get a new leader or something like that. So it can be really challenging and it's never done.
turns.zh: 你怎么带团队？所以团队领导是沟通与影响力很大的一部分。你怎么管理利益相关方？这在增长里很难，因为增长常常被人看成跟精心打磨的产品工艺相对立，但其实不是。这两件事是相辅相成的。所以你真的得靠说服力让别人明白做增长意味着什么。我想说，这是顶点，对吧？这是最难的一项。它是一辈子的旅程。它非常依赖你理解人、理解你在跟谁说话。而这些人每家公司都很不一样，他们看重的「通货」也很不一样。所以这一项，每次你进入一个新角色、新公司、或者换了个新领导，你都得回到原点，重新认识你共事的是谁。所以它真的很有挑战，而且永远做不完。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That component of the competency models, we're the PM of the growth PM role feels like if you were to do these Venn diagram of the two roles, feels like that's a big part of the overlap.
turns.zh: 能力模型里这一块，如果是增长 PM 这个角色，感觉要是把两个角色画成韦恩图，这应该是重叠很大的一部分。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yep, absolutely. There's a lot of overlap between exceptional product managers and exceptional growth practitioners. I think sometimes they just use the skills in different ways. So you need to be great at product strategy to be a product leader, you need to be great at growth strategy to be a growth leader. Just what those things look like can be different between the two. But they're both required skills, required competencies to be exceptional at the role.
turns.zh: 对，绝对。出色的产品经理和出色的增长从业者之间有很多重叠。我想有时候他们只是用技能的方式不同。你要当产品领导，得精通产品战略；要当增长领导，得精通增长战略。只是这两样具体的样子在两者之间可能不同。但它们都是把角色做到极致所必需的技能、必需的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So just to rehash, the four categories are communication influence, growth execution, customer knowledge and growth strategy. You mentioned earlier that people often come to you and they're like, "How do we find another Adam?" And your feedback is one, how do you know that's exactly what you need? And then two, find someone that's up and coming more because it's so hard to find folks like you that are actually ready to take on a head of growth role.
turns.zh: 总结一下，四类是：沟通影响力、增长执行、客户认知、增长战略。你前面提到人们常来找你说「怎么再找一个 Adam？」你的反馈是：第一，你怎么知道这恰好就是你需要的？第二，多找那种正在上升期的人，因为像你这样真的能扛起增长负责人角色的人太难找了。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So a question for you is, one is, do you recommend founders focus on finding someone that's more up and coming and fast learning with a high trajectory? And if so, which of these components would you suggest they look for most?
turns.zh: 所以问你一个问题：一是，你会建议创始人去找那种更有上升势头、学得快、轨迹向上的人吗？如果是，你会建议他们最看重这几项里的哪些？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: One of the challenges of hiring a senior person is that they're all off writing newsletters and making podcast.
turns.zh: 招资深人士的一个难点是，他们都在写 Newsletter、做播客了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Not that we know anybody who does that or anything, but-
turns.zh: 我们又不是认识谁也干这个，不过——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No. That's bullshit. What is that?
turns.zh: 才怪。那是什么鬼。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yeah. So I don't want to right now go back and work at a company again. I'm enjoying what I'm doing and so it's hard to get me, right? But also you don't want me, I think, when you're doing this for the first time. So I think the key there is smart and driven people for sure. Age and youth is a bit relative I'd say. So I would think about hiring somebody who you might say is less experienced in growth, but they could be very senior in another aspect of their career. You can also benefit from hiring somebody internally who wants to branch out into growth. And one of the benefits that you get from that is a lot of time they have one of those competencies really nailed already. Could be like customer knowledge. They might understand your customer base super well because they're already inside the company.
turns.zh: 对。所以我现在不想再回公司上班了。我挺享受现在做的事，所以要找我也难，对吧？而且我觉得，你第一次做这事的时候，其实你也不想要我这种人。所以关键还是聪明、有驱动力的人，这毫无疑问。年龄和资历我倒觉得是相对的。所以我会考虑招那种你可能觉得增长经验少，但在职业别的方面已经很资深的人。你也可以受益于从内部招一个想往增长方向拓展的人。这么做的好处之一是，很多时候他们已经把其中某项能力拿捏得死死的了。比如客户认知。他们可能因为你公司里待着，对你的客户群理解得特别透。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: So if you're going to hire a junior person, the key is, how do you help them learn? And I think if you don't know what you're doing as the founder or the leader, it's hard. You're not going to be able to help them yourself. So you've got to be willing to invest in advisors like me, outside education, mentorship, coaching, otherwise, what's going to happen is that very driven, hungry and enthusiastic person is going to run through a lot of brick walls, which is great, except they're going to miss the fact that the door was standing right next to the wall that they just ran through and you're going to end up with a lot of bricks on the ground.
turns.zh: 所以如果你要招一个初级的人，关键是，你怎么帮他们学？我觉得要是作为创始人或领导，你自己都不知道在干啥，那就难了。你自己帮不了他们。所以你得愿意投资在像我这样的顾问、外部培训、导师、教练上，否则会发生的是：那个特别有冲劲、饥渴又热情的人，会一头撞穿很多砖墙——这本身挺好，只是他们会忽略墙旁边那扇门明明开着，最后地上会留下一堆砖头。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Excellent metaphor.
turns.zh: 绝妙的比喻。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yeah, thank you. And so I have some examples of both hiring people and moving people over in my career. So I think tangible examples are really helpful here. So when I was at Lyft, I had the privilege of hiring that young, smart and driven person a bunch of times, but one of the people who comes to mind is a guy named Ben Lauzier. You should have him on the podcast at some point. He's French, he's very nice to listen to you. He was most recently a VP of product at Thumbtack, but he was definitely not that when I hired him, he was a jack of all trades marketer working at a corporate catering startup when I hired him at Lyft. And he had nailed most of the growth execution and the customer knowledge competencies.
turns.zh: 谢谢。我职业生涯里既有从外部招人的例子，也有内部转岗的例子。所以具体的例子在这里特别有帮助。我在 Lyft 的时候，有幸好几次招到那种年轻、聪明又有冲劲的人，其中一个想到了 Ben Lauzier。你哪天应该请他上播客。他是法国人，听起来很舒服。他最近是 Thumbtack 的产品 VP，但我招他的时候绝对不是这样——我招他时，他是个在餐饮外卖创业公司打杂的市场人员。而增长执行和客户认知这两项能力，他已经拿捏得很好了。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: One was, he was an avid Lyft user himself, so he really understood the product really well. And also, he was just very thoughtful about how he executed, how he experimented. He had done a lot of it and he was very skilled at pulling them off in a very small environment because he had just had to be. And those are the two most important competencies when you're bringing in a younger, earlier stage person because teaching somebody how to execute is not that fun, right? That's a hard skill. The ability to execute is something like executive function skills and things like that. If you haven't developed those by the time you are an adult, I don't know that I'm going to be able to teach you and I'm certainly probably not the right person to teach you. You should definitely get some outside assistance with that. And so I like to get those types of people that have those things if I'm hiring that generally inexperienced growth practitioner.
turns.zh: 一来，他自己就是个狂热的 Lyft 用户，所以对产品理解得非常透。二来，他对怎么执行、怎么做实验特别有想法。他做过很多，而且特别擅长在很小的环境里把事做成，因为不得不如此。而当你招一个更年轻、更早期的人时，这两项就是最重要的能力，因为教一个人怎么执行并不好玩，对吧？那是硬技能。执行力这种东西类似执行功能技能。要是你成年了还没培养出来，我不知道我能不能教会你，我也肯定不是教这个的合适人选。你绝对得找外部帮忙。所以如果要招那种总体没经验的增长从业者，我喜欢招已经具备这些特质的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the two things you said are customer knowledge and execution. Is that the two you said?
turns.zh: 你说的两项是客户认知和执行。就是这两项是吧？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yes. Customer knowledge and growth execution. And so let me tell you an execution story about Ben really quick. This comes also down to work ethic too. So we interviewed Ben and it was a long day of interviews in a tiny glass conference room and Lyft was, I don't know, 30 people or something at the time. At one of the interview breaks, Ben had come over and he didn't have his computer and anything like that. And so he was ducking out of work to do the interview. And he actually came out of the office and he's like, "Hey, does anybody have a computer that I can borrow?" And so we gave him this old crappy Chromebook and I was like, "Why do you need a computer?" And he's like, "I have to go edit this file and do this thing and check something in at work and deploy this thing or whatever."
turns.zh: 对。客户认知和增长执行。我快速讲个 Ben 的执行故事。这也关系到职业操守。我们面 Ben 那天，在一间小玻璃会议室里面了一整天。Lyft 当时好像也就 30 来人。中间一次面试间隙，Ben 走过来，没带电脑什么的，他是溜出来上班来面试的。他走出办公室说「嘿，谁有电脑能借我一下？」我们就给了他一台很破的旧 Chromebook，我问「你要电脑干嘛？」他说「我得去改个文件、处理个事、把公司的东西提交上线之类的」。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And I'm like, "Wow, this is a guy that really knows how to get stuff done and is so much so that he's pausing his interview process so that he could go get a thing done for his company that he's actively trying to leave, but he's got this work ethic and this execution." And that really stuck with me. And he probably would remember this story if we brought it up. So the time he borrowed a crappy Chromebook laptop to do work at the job that he was trying to leave.
turns.zh: 我当时就想「哇，这是个真知道怎么把事搞定的人，以至于他连面试过程都暂停一下，去把正要离职的那家公司的事儿给办了——但他就有这种职业操守和执行力」。这让我印象特别深。要是我们现在提起来，他大概也记得。就是他借了台破 Chromebook，去办正想离职那家公司活儿的那次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are the chances that was staged?
turns.zh: 这有多大可能是提前安排好的？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: He seemed very innocent. So I think not staged.
turns.zh: 他看起来特别单纯。所以我觉着不是演的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great.
turns.zh: 好，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: But I could be wrong. But now everyone that interviews that is going to ask to borrow a laptop and-
turns.zh: 不过我也可能是错的。但现在每个来面试的人都会问借笔记本，然后——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: ... check in some work.
turns.zh: ……提交点活儿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The phone call.
turns.zh: 电话响。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: "Adam, I need to fix something."
turns.zh: 「Adam，我得修个东西。」

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: That's right. So that's Ben. And then on the other side, and I'll cover this one really quickly, and the other side of moving somebody over internally, I had equally great success with that. So there was another person named Sean at Patreon who was a marketer, again, a jack of all trades marketer. And I think I have a propensity and a bias towards folks like that because that's one of the ways that I started my career was in marketing. But anyways, I moved him over from marketing to being a growth PM, an entry level growth PM.
turns.zh: 没错。这就是 Ben。另一面，我快速讲一下，就是内部转岗，那一面我也同样成功过。Patreon 有个人叫 Sean，也是个打杂市场人员。我想我对这类人有偏好和倾向，因为这恰恰是我职业生涯起步的方式——从市场做起。总之，我把他从市场转成了增长 PM，入门级的增长 PM。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And he had a ton of the execution skills, ability to prioritize really well and customer knowledge skills as well, more so on the customer side because he was an internal transfer, so he really knew our customers. He'd spent tons of time talking to people, studying data and things like that. And he had really great fluency with data and a drive to continue improving his ability to access and pull out insights and information. And so he turned out to be really great, but just a very different profile of a person than Ben was. And here's an internal hire versus an external hire.
turns.zh: 他有一大堆执行技能，排序能力特别好，也有客户认知技能——更多在客户侧，因为他是内部转岗，所以特别懂我们的客户。他花大量时间跟人聊、研究数据之类的。而且他对数据特别熟练，也有持续打磨自己提取洞察和信息能力的冲劲。所以他最后表现特别好，只是人物画像跟 Ben 很不一样。这里是内部招聘对外部招聘。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: So you can have success with both, but I think you really have to make sure that there's some foundational things that are in place like that ability to get customer knowledge and execute.
turns.zh: 所以两条路都能成，但我觉得你真得确保一些基础的东西到位了，比如那种获取客户认知和执行的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If a founder is listening and trying to decide or hiring a head of growth or a new growth person, would you push them one way or the other, internal hire versus finding someone up and coming and smart?
turns.zh: 如果有个创始人正在听，想要决定或者正在招增长负责人、新的增长人员，你会更推其中哪条路，内部招聘还是找一个上升期、聪明的人？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: I tend to skew more towards internal hire to be perfectly honest, because I believe in creating opportunity inside a company. I think it's not done often enough. And I also believe that helping people transition into new roles is a way to get more people into the practice. And one of the ways that can happen is if you take a chance on somebody who has demonstrated a good track record in some other aspect of your business. So I tend to recommend internal. I think you have faster time to results. I think you know what you're getting better and in much less likelihood of making the wrong hire there. So I bias towards internal hires.
turns.zh: 老实说，我更偏向内部招聘，因为我相信在公司内部创造机会。我觉得这事做得还不够多。而且我也相信，帮人转到新角色，是让更多人进入这个领域的方式。其中一个办法就是，你给那个在业务别的方面已经证明了自己的人一个机会。所以我倾向推荐内部。我觉得你出结果更快。你更清楚会得到什么，招错人的可能性也小得多。所以我偏向内部招聘。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And I think partly, I feel that too because there's so much content and training for growth these days that somebody has that background in your company and is already motivated and excited and then can just learn, go to Reforge course, read certain newsletters, feels like it's a lot easier to ramp up. Except, I always feel like if you need someone for SEO or paid growth, that's a hard thing to learn. What's your take there?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我想部分原因也是因为，现在增长方面的内容和培训这么多，公司里有人有那个背景、本来就很有动力很兴奋，然后只要去学——上 Reforge 的课、读某些 Newsletter——感觉上手容易多了。只是我总觉得，如果你需要有人做 SEO 或者付费增长，那是很难学的事。你怎么看？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: I would bucket that type of person into a specialist. And one of the archetypes that I talk about is this idea of the painter versus the architect versus the surgeon. And the surgeon is your precision person. I don't actually recommend hiring that as your first hire, but when you are onto something and you really need expertise and you don't have that expertise internally, yes, I think hiring externally is the right thing to do at that point because those are really specific skills that some people have taken years to learn. And I can't just teach someone SEO over the course of a weekend and expect that they're really going to get it. In those cases, I think hiring that specialist or that surgeon is the right approach, once you've got some of the foundational stuff in place.
turns.zh: 我会把那种人归为专家型。我讲过的几种原型里，有一个「画匠 vs 建筑师 vs 外科医生」的说法。外科医生就是你的精准型人才。其实我不建议把这种人作为你的第一个招聘，但当你已经摸到门道、真的需要专业知识、而内部又没有，那对，我觉得这时候从外部招是对的，因为那些是非常具体的技能，有些人花了多少年才学会。我不可能一个周末就把 SEO 教给一个人，还指望他真懂。在这些情况下，我觉得招那个专家、那个外科医生是对的，前提是你已经把一些基础的东西搭好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Great. Yeah, it feels like there's still a lot of dark art in those two specialties that take years of experience.
turns.zh: 太棒了。对。感觉这两项专业里还是有很多「黑魔法」，得靠多年经验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a good time to segue to our second topic, which is onboarding. I know you're a big proponent of spending time on onboarding, optimizing onboarding. How have you found onboarding to be as a lever for growth and just what gets you excited about investing in onboarding?
turns.zh: 这正好过渡到我们的第二个话题：引导流程。我知道你是花时间在引导、优化引导的大拥护者。你发现引导作为增长杠杆效果如何？是什么让你对投资引导流程这么兴奋？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: I love onboarding. I probably do at least an onboarding project to at least one with every company that I've worked for and a lot that I advise. The first thing I would say is, onboarding is the only part of your product experience that a hundred percent of people are ever going to touch. Good luck getting a hundred percent feature adoption of anything else in your product right? But onboarding is the thing that you have to go through in order to use the product. It's also the first opportunity that you have as a company to deliver on the promise that you made out in the marketplace.
turns.zh: 我超爱引导。我基本上在每一家工作过的公司、还有很多我顾问的公司，都至少做过一个引导项目。首先我想说，引导是你产品体验里唯一一个百分之百的用户都会触碰到的部分。你想让产品里其他任何功能的采用率达到百分之百？祝你好运，对吧？但引导是用户为了用你的产品必须经过的一关。它也是你作为一家公司，第一次有机会去兑现你在市场上做出的承诺。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: So I like to think of your brand is the promise that you're making and your product experience is your delivery of that promise. And those two things have to be in lockstep with each other or you're going to have mismatched expectations and some really disappointed customers. So this is the first chance that a customer has to be really excited or really disappointed in what they thought they were getting. So don't mess that up.
turns.zh: 所以我喜欢这么想：你的品牌就是你做出的承诺，而你的产品体验就是你兑现承诺的方式。这两件事必须步调一致，否则用户的期待就会错位，然后你就会收获一批大失所望的客户。这是客户第一次有机会对自己以为能得到的产品感到兴奋或者失望。所以千万别搞砸了。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And the third thing I would say is it's also probably the most motivated that someone is going to be about your product since they're typically starting their onboarding journey with you at a time where they're like, "I need this thing really badly that you're selling." And so they're really motivated, right? And so it's an opportunity for you to put some friction in place and learn a lot about them because they will knock down doors to get to your product. So that's why I think it's a super powerful lever for growth. And we worked on this extensively at Lyft, at Patreon, Wyzant, Imperfect Foods just released some onboarding improvements that we had created when I was there, which was nice to see that finally come to light. So yeah, I've done this pretty much everywhere at some point.
turns.zh: 我要说的第三点是，这也是一个人对你的产品最有动力的时候，因为他们通常开始引导旅程时，正是「我特别需要你卖的这个东西」的时刻。所以他们动力十足，对吧？所以这是你设置一点摩擦、多了解他们的好机会，因为他们会撞破门也要用上你的产品。所以这就是为什么我觉得它是超级有力的增长杠杆。我们在 Lyft、Patreon、Wyzant 都大量做过这个，Imperfect Foods 最近上线了我们当时做的引导改进——看到它终于面世挺好。所以基本上我在每家公司某个时候都做过这事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What impact have you seen from working on onboarding to give people a sense of like, "Wow, this is what I can get if I put some time here."
turns.zh: 你从做引导上看到过什么影响，让人有那种「哇，我在这花点时间就能得到这种效果」的感觉？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yeah. One of the things that onboarding really drives is habit formation with the product, which leads to retention. And so you should expect to improve your overall cohort retention curves by focusing on the onboarding and activation experience. I have seen companies shift their curve outward by 10, 15, 20 percentage points from making those changes, especially when you consider that churn is most likely to happen in the very earliest usage of the product. If you can get people past that hump, it's a really invaluable part of the product to work on.
turns.zh: 对。引导真正驱动的一件事，是产品在用户身上形成习惯，进而带来留存。所以你应该预期，聚焦在引导和激活体验上，能改善你的整体同期留存曲线。我见过有公司靠这些改动，把曲线往外推了 10、15、20 个百分点，尤其是考虑到流失最可能发生在产品最早使用的阶段。如果你能让人跨过那个坎，那就是产品里极其宝贵的一块。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: So I'll give you a really concrete example. At Patreon, one of the places we worked on onboarding really extensively and the onboarding experience was one of the teams that we had on growth at Patreon. We did a lot of experimentation around the earliest, what we would call product led sales now, when do you connect a human being with a creator and the onboarding experience and what is that impact and how do you connect them with the right person or with the right creator when there are tens of thousands going through that onboarding journey every week?
turns.zh: 我给你一个很具体的例子。在 Patreon，我们有一支团队大量做引导，引导体验是 Patreon 增长团队里的一个组。我们围绕最早的、现在叫「产品驱动销售」做了很多实验：什么时候把一个人和真人、和创作者连起来，跟引导体验结合，影响是什么，当每周有几万人走引导流程时，你怎么把他们跟对的人、对的创作者连起来？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: What we realized through a lot of experimentation was the idea of connecting someone with a human being the right person at the right time would improve the first month of revenue or the second month of revenue that a creator made on the platform by 25%. Why that mattered is because the second month that you processed payments on the platform was a key input into your LTV on the platform. So by improving a creator's first and second month revenue by 25%, we were then able to improve their overall value on Patreon by an equivalent amount, which is pretty massive. Moving anything by 25% is really impressive.
turns.zh: 我们通过大量实验发现：在对的时间把对的人跟真人连起来，能让一个创作者在平台上第一个月或第二个月的收入提升 25%。这为什么重要？因为你在平台上处理支付的第二个月，是你平台 LTV 的一个关键输入。所以把一个创作者的第一个月和第二个月收入提升 25%，我们就能等量地提升他在 Patreon 上的整体价值，这相当可观。把任何东西动 25% 都很厉害。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And so that was human intervention, and then we actually started to productize the stuff that the humans were doing. And so what is not scalable when you're using people becomes very scalable if you can replicate components of that with technology. And so that was the next phase, so we get back to that growth execution thing that I talked about and productizing learnings. That is an example of how you go from, we've learned some things by humans that have made a 25% impact to now we're building these into the product. And so that's a really good example I think, of Patreon and one of the impacts that we had on creator, earnings, retention and their overall success on the platform.
turns.zh: 这先是人工干预，然后我们开始把人做的事产品化。所以你用人的时候不可扩展，但如果你能用技术复制其中的组件，它就变得非常可扩展。于是这就进入了下一阶段，又回到我讲的增长执行和「把经验产品化」。这就是你怎么从「人做出了一些有 25% 影响的事」走到「现在把这些建进产品里」。所以我觉得这是 Patreon 一个很好的例子，也是我们当时对创作者的收入、留存和整体成功产生的一个影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an amazing example, in case it's useful to a person working on the onboarding. Can you share any more about what you actually did there? You create some algorithm of this type of person, we'll connect them to a person and then you productize it. Is there anything more you could share there that might be useful to folks?
turns.zh: 这例子太棒了。要是对正在做引导的人有用，你能多分享一点你们当时实际做了什么吗？你做了某种「这种人用算法连到人」然后产品化。有没有更多能分享、对大家有用的？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Gosh, we did so much. So I'll try to pull out a couple of example. So one of the things that we did, and again, I spoke to the fact that people are really motivated in your onboarding experience, one of the first things we did was we tried to identify better who a creator was in the onboarding experience. And who they were meant how big is their audience on a bunch of the channels where they managed communities, Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, Discord, YouTube, et cetera. And then how engaged was that audience? It's one thing if you make crazy cat videos on YouTube and you have a million subscribers, it's another thing if every time you publish a video, all million of those people watch it, comment on it, share it, et cetera.
turns.zh: 天，我们做了太多。我挑几个例子。我们做的一件事，再说一遍，我在引导体验里人动力最足——我们最先做的，是更好识别引导里一个创作者是谁。他们是谁，指的是他们在管理社群的各个渠道上有多大受众，Twitter、Facebook、Instagram、Discord、YouTube 等等。然后这个受众有多活跃？你在 YouTube 上做疯狂猫片、有一百万订阅，是一回事；你每次发视频，这一百万人都看、都评论、都转发，是另一回事。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And so we would ask creators to connect various accounts to Patreon, maybe through authoring with YouTube or Spotify or Instagram or Facebook or something like that, Twitter, and then we would pull in the data into our backend and identify people who had large followings and also heavily engaged followings, based on a set of criteria per channel. And again, this was not just like me inventing this. We had a data scientist team that we worked very closely with to figure out what was important and what wasn't in this model. And then if you were one of those people that had a high propensity for success, high potential creators, we would siphon them off from the regular self-guided onboarding and basically land them in the lap of a human being who could engage with them, reach out, get them even more excited and start talking to them about the best things to do.
turns.zh: 于是我们会让创作者把各种账号连到 Patreon，可能通过 YouTube、Spotify、Instagram、Facebook、Twitter 的授权，然后把数据拉进我们的后台，按每个渠道的一套标准，识别出那些有大粉丝量、而且粉丝高度活跃的人。再说一遍，这不是我拍脑袋想的。我们有一个数据科学团队，跟我们紧密合作，搞清楚这个模型里什么重要、什么不重要。然后如果你是高成功倾向、高潜力创作者之一，我们会把你从常规的自助引导里分流出，基本丢到一个真人怀里，他能跟你互动、主动联系、让你更兴奋，开始跟你聊该做哪些最好的事。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And then the productization of that, the best things to do turned out to be things like one of our product principles, which became opinionated defaults, which is basically making it hard to do the wrong thing when you're setting up your Patreon page and easy to do the right thing but not eliminating choice.
turns.zh: 然后那部分的产品化：那些「最好的事」，最后变成了我们的一条产品原则，叫「有主见的默认值」——基本就是在你设置 Patreon 页面时，让做错事变难、做对事变易，但不取消选择。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: So the creator could still make the choice to do the wrong thing. They could still set up a single tier when we knew that a three-tiered pricing model actually would work better for them, or they could choose to set up 40 tiers when we knew that the sweet spot was three to five or perhaps make their lowest price tier a dollar instead of what we recommended, which was like three or $5 entry points. So they could do all that stuff, but we made it difficult for them to do it. We put more friction in place when they were trying to change some of those defaults because we had learned across a universe of creators, hundreds of thousands of people what worked best.
turns.zh: 所以创作者仍然可以选择做错事。他们仍然可以设成单一档位，尽管我们知道三层定价模型对他们其实更好；或者他们可以设成 40 个档位，而我们知道甜区是三到五个；又或者把最低档设成一美元，而不是我们推荐的比如三或五美元入门价。这些他们都能做，但我们让做这些变难了。当他们想改那些默认值时，我们加了更多摩擦，因为我们在成千上万、几十万创作者身上学到了什么最有效。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And so putting in those guardrails and those default things was a huge lever for us to drive the behavior that we wanted. And again, we learned that from human intervention with the right types of creators, then detecting those people and putting in the guardrails in the product themselves and making those recommendations inside the product experience. And they were pricing tier structure, how you actually write your page, all of that stuff.
turns.zh: 所以设置那些护栏和默认值，对我们来说是驱动想要行为的一个巨大杠杆。再说一遍，这是我们从对正确类型创作者的人工干预里学到的，然后识别那些人、在产品里加上护栏、并在产品体验里给出那些推荐。涉及定价档位结构、你页面到底怎么写，所有那些东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a great example. It reminds me we had exactly the same situation at Airbnb that you just made me think about. We called it smart defaults. What was your term? Opinionated defaults?
turns.zh: 太好的例子。这让我想起我们在 Airbnb 有过完全一样的情况，你刚让我想到。我们叫它「智能默认值」。你那个词叫什么？有主见的默认值？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Opinionated defaults. Yeah.
turns.zh: 有主见的默认值。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I like that. So at Airbnb we had a bunch of calendar settings when a host signs up, on the host side is where I spent a lot of my time, we had instant book, which is basically you sign up as a host and people can book you instantly. That became the default for Airbnb. And so to make that successful, hosts had to have their calendar be accurate from the beginning. And so what we got to eventually, is we tried to figure out, are you a professional host that knows what you're doing? Are you a mom and pop that's just trying this out? And then based on that, either block your entire calendar, keep it all open, or somewhere in between.
turns.zh: 对，我喜欢这说法。在 Airbnb，房东注册时有一堆日历设置——我大量时间花在房东端——我们有「即时预订」，基本就是你注册成房东，别人就能立刻订你。这成了 Airbnb 的默认。而要让它成功，房东从一开始就得把日历弄准。所以我们最后做的是，先搞清楚：你是个知道自己在干啥的职业房东？还是只是试试看的小本经营？然后据此，要么锁掉整本日历，要么全开放，要么取中间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's interesting that it connects to your point about, and I was going to come back to this that, a lot of people think of onboarding as a conversion opportunity and it definitely is. But to your point, even more interestingly, it's a retention opportunity because in the Airbnb case, hosts sign up, they get booked for a day, they don't want to host, they're like, "Shit, what the hell's going on here? I'm out."
turns.zh: 有意思的是这连上了你说的点——我本来也想回到这——很多人把引导当成转化机会，它当然是。但如你所说，更有意思的是，它也是留存机会，因为在 Airbnb 的例子里，房东注册了、被订了一天、不想做了，就会「靠，这什么情况？我不干了」。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so, I wanted to ask you, how should folks think about onboarding conversion versus retention, and why is it so powerful for retention?
turns.zh: 所以我想问你，大家该怎么看待引导的「转化 vs 留存」，为什么它对留存这么有力？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: I actually think if you're doing it right, sometimes conversion should actually decrease a little bit. So you might actually have fewer people getting all the way through successfully, but I think that's okay because a lot of those people were probably not the right people for your product, which means they wouldn't have been engaged customers, they probably would have churned. So just by the nature of actually weeding out some people, you're going to improve retention because the people who are going through are the people who are much more highly qualified. And so I think that's also why onboarding is so challenging because you have to figure out what that sweet spot is, right?
turns.zh: 我其实觉得，如果你做对了，有时候转化还应该稍微降一点。所以真正走完流程的人可能更少，但我觉得这没事，因为那些人里很多本来就不是你产品的对的人，也就是说他们不会是投入的客户，大概会流失。所以光凭把一些人筛掉这个性质，你就能改善留存，因为走完流程的是那些资质高得多的人。所以我觉得这也是引导这么难的原因，因为你得找到那个甜区，对吧？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: You could actually reduce conversion to a point where it's not offset by improvements in retention and you'd be doing the wrong thing. So when you're experimenting, you have to look at these push and pull metrics of these opposing metrics. But overall, I find that the biggest impact that you'll have is on retaining users because you are trying to connect them to the value that your product offers and form a habit. And if you form that habit early on, they're going to stick around because they're going to get it, they're going to get the benefit of the product, and they're going to be excited to stay and then tell more people about it. So that's why I think it's a much bigger impact on retention than conversion.
turns.zh: 你可能把转化降到一个点，已经没法被留存的提升抵消了，那你就做错了。所以做实验时，你得看这些相互拉扯的指标、这些对立指标。但总的来说，我发现你最大的影响在留住用户上，因为你在试着把他们连到产品提供的价值上、形成习惯。如果你早点形成那个习惯，他们就会留下来，因为他们会懂、会拿到产品的好处、会兴奋地留下并告诉更多人。所以这就是为什么我觉得它对留存的影响远大于对转化的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Obviously retention is a longer tail metric and conversion is immediate.
turns.zh: 显然留存是个长尾指标，转化是即时的。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have any tips for folks that are like, "Oh my God, how do I know if this conversion hit is worth retention increasing potentially?"
turns.zh: 你有没有什么建议给那种「天，我怎么知道这次转化下滑值不值得可能换来的留存提升」的人？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yeah. I think the answer is not wait 90 days to find out, right? Nobody has that time. And so what I tend to do is look at proxy metrics. So there are proxies for things like 90 day retention. As an example at Patreon, one of our proxies around the eventual success of a creator was how quickly they would reach certain dollar thresholds once they launched. And so your velocity to get to your first patron, your first a hundred dollars processed on the platform and that thing had a lot to do with how big and successful you would be, and therefore how well you would retain.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得答案不是等 90 天看结果，对吧？没人有那时间。所以我习惯看代理指标。90 天留存是有代理指标的。比如在 Patreon，一个创作者最终成不成功的一个代理，是他们上线后多快达到某些金额门槛。所以你拿到第一个赞助人、在平台上处理第一笔一百美元的速度，跟你能做多大、多成功，因而也跟你能留存多好，关系很大。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And so we looked at very early signals to understand and evaluate how good someone was going to be. We also did a lot of qualitative screening in the beginning. So as people went through, we would take samplings of creators who were onboarding and signing up and launching their pages, and we would actually look at who the creator was and what they were doing. And then we would be able to run it through our model to say, "It looks like we're getting a lot of the right people going through and doing the right behaviors, therefore, we're very confident that they're going to retain better and do the right things." So yeah, proxy metrics are the key there.
turns.zh: 所以我们看很早的信号来理解、评估一个人会有多好。一开始我们也做了很多定性筛查。当人走流程时，我们会抽样那些正在引导、注册、上线的创作者，实际去看这个创作者是谁、在做什么。然后我们能用模型跑一下说「看起来进来的人里很多都是对的人、在做对的行为，所以我们很有信心他们会留存得更好、做对的事」。所以代理指标是关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So part of this is find this leading indicator proxy metric, and then to your point, maybe build a little bit of a heuristic that's like, okay, this is qualitatively looking like it's doing the right things to our new users.
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以一部分是找到这个先行指标、代理指标，然后如你所说，也许建一点启发式规则，比如「好，定性上看，我们新用户在做对的事」。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe our last question on onboarding is, at Airbnb and I imagine many companies, there's this constant desire to, "Let's just redo this whole thing. Let's just redesign it. Let's start again." And my question to you is just, how much is too much on redoing, rethinking, onboarding, optimizing, micro-optimizing? Any answers there?
turns.zh: 关于引导，也许我们最后一个问题是：在 Airbnb、我想在很多公司，都有这种持续的冲动「我们把整个重做一遍、重新设计、从头来」。我的问题就是，重做、重构、优化、微优化，多少算太多？有什么答案吗？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yeah. I would say first, I very strongly dislike the idea of redesigning something for redesigning sake. So I think that it is true that you should spend a lot of time on onboarding, and you should regularly revisit it as you learn new things about your users. So even at Patreon, we would work on onboarding and then we take a beat, we'd let it go for a while, improved, and then as we learn new things, we would find ways to fold those back into onboarding. So I find that it's acceptable to revisit when you are learning net new principles about your customers or something new about your growth model where onboarding can directly influence.
turns.zh: 对。我会说首先，我极度讨厌「为了重设计而重设计」。所以我认为确实该在引导上花很多时间，也该随着你对用户学到新东西而定期重访它。即使在 Patreon，我们会做引导，然后停一下，放它跑一阵、改进了，等学到新东西，我们再找办法把那些折回到引导里。所以我觉得，当你学到关于客户的全新原则、或者增长模型里引导能直接影响的新东西时，重访是可以接受的。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: So as we learned at Patreon what the right tier construction was, or the right way to talk about your Patreon page or the right way to message it in the beginning, we would go back and say, "How do we build this newfound knowledge into an experience that sets someone up for success?" But if we weren't gaining new insights, we weren't just tweaking the onboarding experience and trying to tune it in a very micro way, because the reality is, that doesn't really move the needle that often, especially once you've got it in a pretty good foundational place. And only when you discover something really fundamentally net new, will it have an outsized impact on retention or the success of early users. So don't just redesign for redesign sake, make sure there's a new hard earned insight that you've got before you do it.
turns.zh: 所以当我们在 Patreon 学到正确的档位结构该是什么、正确的聊 Patreon 页面的方式、开头正确的 messaging，我们会回去说「我们怎么把这份新发现的知识建进一个让人成功的体验里？」但如果我们没获得新洞察，我们不会只是微调引导体验、试图非常微观地去调，因为现实是，那不常真的动指针——尤其在你已经把它放到一个相当不错的基础位置之后。只有当你发现真正根本性的全新东西，它才会对留存或早期用户的成功有超常的影响。所以别为了重设计而重设计，确保你动手前真的有新挣来的洞察。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you think at scale companies, I don't know, maybe after hundreds of people, they should have a team, like an onboarding optimization team? I find that often is true. And I guess, do you think that makes sense?
turns.zh: 你觉得在成规模的公司，我不知道，也许几百人之后，他们该有个团队，比如引导优化团队？我发现常常确实如此。我想，你觉得这合理吗？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yeah. I think it's very helpful. And the reason I think it's helpful is because I do think it's easy to walk away from onboarding because there's so many other things to work on and to lose sight of the fact this is such a critical part of the experience. And I don't know how many times I've come into a company and they're like, "Yeah, we built that a long time ago and we've never looked at it again. It's been a few years, but we're really having a real problem with retention and people dropping off in the first seven days." And I'm like, "Yeah, I think it's time we take another look at the onboarding experience. Products change quite a bit. Maybe people are getting something that's different than they expect, or maybe we know a lot more that we can use to influence decisions that they make."
turns.zh: 对。我觉得很有帮助。我觉得有帮助的原因是，引导很容易被放下，因为有太多别的事要做，然后就忘了这是体验里这么关键的一部分。我不记得多少次进一家公司，他们说「对，我们很久以前建的，之后再没看过。几年了，但我们真的在留存上有大问题，头七天人就掉。」我就说「对，我觉得是时候再看看引导体验了。产品变了不少。也许人们拿到的跟预期不一样，也许我们知道的多得多，可以用来影响他们做的决定。」

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: So I do think it is beneficial to have that team, or at least a team, that part of their job is the activation experience and therefore some part of their roadmap is working on onboarding and then other aspects of activation. So it may not be what they work on 12 months out of the year, but maybe for a quarter or two in a given year.
turns.zh: 所以我确实觉得有个团队、或者至少一个团队，把激活体验当成工作的一部分是有益的，所以他们路线图的某部分在做引导、以及激活的其他方面。所以可能不是一年 12 个月都在做，而是某一年里的那么一两个季度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. And there's a LinkedIn post you wrote with a bunch of examples of onboarding work you've done. So we're going to include them in the show notes for folks that are-
turns.zh: 酷。你写过一篇 LinkedIn 帖子，带了一堆你做过的引导例子。我们打算把它们放进节目笔记，给那些——

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Nice.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... hoping for more examples. Yeah. Okay. Third topic, final topic is around company selection and evaluating where to work. And you have this really cool framework that I think you call PMF for candidates. Can you talk about what that is and then we'll get into it a little bit?
turns.zh: ……想要更多例子的人。好。第三个话题，也是最后一个，是关于公司选择、评估去哪工作。你有一个超酷的框架，我想你叫它「求职者的 PMF」。能讲讲这是什么，然后我们深入一点吗？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Yeah. I somehow stumbled on that name and it just made sense because of the acronym. But I think I was really motivated to revisit this because as we know in tech there's been a ton of layoffs and very public layoffs because of the economy, the state of funding, things like that. And I don't think we're done yet. I think we're pretty far from being done. But it's really important, and I've been burned by this a few times, to put some power back in the hands of the people who are actually seeking the jobs to understand what are some criteria that are important and these are the criteria that are important to me that help you make decisions about which company I should join, assuming they'll have me. And so the PMF acronym, and we're all familiar with product-market fit, right?
turns.zh: 对。我不知怎么碰出这个名字，因为缩写刚好说得通。但我想我重访这个的动机很强，是因为如我们所知，科技圈因为经济、融资环境等等，有大量、而且很公开的裁员。而且我觉得还没完。我觉得离完还远。但这真的很重要，而且我被坑过几次——要把一些权力放回真正找工作的人手里，让他们理解哪些标准重要，而这些是对我重要的标准，帮你决定该加入哪家公司（假设他们要我）。所以 PMF 这个缩写，我们都熟悉产品市场契合（product-market fit），对吧？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: So in a way it's both the product-market fit for as a candidate with the company, but then also PMF stands for people, mission and financials. And these are my three criteria. They may not be yours, Lenny, or they might not be the average person on the street, but the point is that you should have a set of criteria that you are unapologetically rigorous around and you should learn how to evaluate companies against that set of criteria. First, I guess I'll tell you what by people, mission and financials.
turns.zh: 所以一方面，它是求职者跟公司的产品市场契合；但另一方面，PMF 代表 People（人）、Mission（使命）、Financials（财务）。这是我的三个标准。可能不全是你的，Lenny，也不一定是街上普通人的，但重点是，你该有一套你理直气壮地严格对待的标准，并学会用那套标准评估公司。先说我说的人、使命、财务各指什么。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: So people are these folks that I am going to enjoy working with everyday that I'm going to be able to have hard conversations with, that I'm going to be able to disagree with and work through those disagreements and feel better on the other side of that productive disagreement, for example, and get to resolutions. What do I think about my peer set, the leaders, the people below me, if that's the role I'm stepping into, et cetera. So that's the people dimension.
turns.zh: 人，是我每天会乐意共事的人，是能跟我有艰难对话的人，是能跟我意见不合、一起把分歧捋顺、在那场有建设性的分歧之后感觉更好、并达成结论的人。我对我的同侪、领导、我下面的人（如果我要进的是那个角色）怎么看，等等。这是人的维度。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Mission, which is critically important for me, is that if I join a company and I do my job, which often involves growing that company really big, getting a lot of customers, generating a lot of demand and retention and stuff, I want to make sure that a lot of people have a better outcome in life because of that company's existence. And I don't just mean employees and founders having a good financial outcome, which I think is important. But I also mean in the case of creators on Patreon, we were building a new way for creators to make money, which they could then use to hire people, create more jobs, make better content, and live their life in a sustainable way so that they weren't a starving artist and they weren't living paycheck to paycheck. So that's really important, the mission aspect, that's got to exist.
turns.zh: 使命，对我极其重要，意思是如果我加入一家公司、把工作做了——通常包含把公司做得很大、拿到很多客户、产生很多需求和留存之类的——我想确保因为这家公司的存在，很多人在生活里有更好的结果。我不只是指员工和创始人有好的财务结果，那当然重要。我还指，比如 Patreon 上的创作者，我们在建一种创作者赚钱的新方式，他们能用来雇人、创造更多就业、做更好的内容，并以可持续的方式生活，这样他们就不是穷艺术家、不是月光族。所以使命这块真的很重要，它必须存在。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And then the third one is, and I think really important now is this idea of financials or fiscal discipline. You've got a lot of companies who raised boatloads of money or did financial planning during the peak of the pandemic and assumed that their business was going to continue operating at the pace that it was operating forever. A lot of those companies are running out of money, they've seen a hit to demand and they've had to lay people off as a result or make really big strategic swings.
turns.zh: 第三是，我觉得现在特别重要的，是「财务/财务纪律」这个概念。很多公司在疫情高峰时融了大笔钱、做了财务规划，假设他们的业务会永远以那个速度跑下去。很多这样的公司钱快烧光了，需求受打击，结果不得不裁员或者做很大的战略转向。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: There are plenty of companies that you're not really hearing about that were more conservative in their approach, that understood and were able to look into the future and be really responsible with their money. And those people are not laying off employees. And so they're not all over LinkedIn talking about it because they're not laying people off. There's no hashtag layoff for them. So that's what by financials. And so that's the PMF framework and evaluating across those dimensions is super important. I've done it two times in the last 10 to 15 years, and I've done it poorly, two times in the last 15 years. And Lyft and Patreon are two times where I've done it really well. Wyzant and Imperfect Foods are two times where I personally don't think I've done a good enough job evaluating.
turns.zh: 也有很多你其实没怎么听说的公司，做法更保守，能看向未来、对钱非常负责。那些公司不裁员。所以他们不会满 LinkedIn 都在谈这事，因为他们没裁。他们没那个 #裁员 标签。所以这就是财务的意思。这就是 PMF 框架，跨这些维度评估超级重要。过去 10 到 15 年里我做过两次，做得很差；过去 15 年里我也做过两次，做得好。Lyft 和 Patreon 是我做得很好的两次。Wyzant 和 Imperfect Foods 是我个人觉得评估得不够好的两次。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Any time where I've shortcutted my criteria, where I've settled for two out of three, or thought one was great, when really it wasn't, has not ended well for me, for the company, it's not that the company imploded, but I found myself out of a job or really frustrated and burned out or something like that. I already talked about the Wyzant example where we had to lay off a bunch of people because the founders expected something very different than what I expected to be able to deliver, that's a big people miss. And Imperfect Foods was somewhat similar, amazing mission, really great financial strategy, fantastic CFO, but a lot of infighting at the C-suite. And it made it really difficult for us to plan and move the company forward together because people were at odds with each other all the time and not resolving disagreements productively. And when that happens, it's hard to be a product or a growth leader because you bear the brunt of the angst that people have. So anyway, so those are a couple examples and some of the characteristics of PMF.
turns.zh: 任何一次我抄了近路、满足于三取二、或者以为某一项很好其实不是，结果对我、对公司都不好——不是说公司垮了，而是我发现自己丢了工作、或者极度沮丧burnout之类的。Wyzant 的例子我讲过了，因为创始人的预期和我能交付的完全不同，我们不得不裁一堆人，那是人在维度上的大失误。Imperfect Foods 有点类似，使命超棒、财务战略超好、CFO 超棒，但 C  Suite 里内斗严重。这让我们很难一起规划、推进公司，因为人一直在互相对立、不建设性地解决分歧。那种时候，做产品或增长领导很难，因为你得承受别人焦虑的冲击。总之，这是几个例子，也是 PMF 的一些特征。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In the case of Imperfect Foods, what could you have done to have avoided that issue and seen if it was true PMF?
turns.zh: 以 Imperfect Foods 为例，你本来能做什么来避免那个问题、看清它是不是真 PMF？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: I would have tried to observe the inner workings of the C-Suite a little bit more closely before I accepted an offer to join the company. I would've attended an executive meeting or joined them on an offsite. And I think, too often, candidates don't feel like they can ask for those things. And it's true, if you're entering the C-suite, you're going to ask for more stuff, you're more experienced. But I also think that's true of a junior employee. You can observe a team meeting, you can observe a product review and understand, you sign an NDA, you promise you won't tell anybody about it, but observe what is happening and the dynamics of that room. Who's doing the talking? How feedback is delivered, is it constructive? Is it antagonistic, et cetera. So you can observe and then you can also ask questions.
turns.zh: 我会努力在我接受 offer 加入之前，更近距离地观察 C-Suite 的内部运作。我会去列席一次高管会议，或者跟他们一起参加 offsite。我觉得候选人常常不敢要求这些。确实，如果你进 C-Suite，你会要更多东西，你更资深。但我觉得对一个初级员工也一样。你可以观察一次团队会议，你可以观察一次产品评审，去理解——你签个 NDA，承诺不告诉任何人——但观察那个房间里在发生什么、 dynamics 是什么。谁在说话？反馈怎么给的，是建设性的？还是对抗性的？等等。所以你可以观察，也可以问问题。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: So questions that I like to ask are, tell me about the last strategic offsite that you had as a leadership team. Where do people disagree? What was one thing that they disagreed on and where did you end up on that point and how did you get there? And I actually ask them to tell me, it's like a reverse behavioral interview question. I ask them to tell me how they navigated it, and I will ask the CEO that and really dig in on that particular set of questions. Those are the things that I do to evaluate the people dimension, which is one of the hardest, I will say. Financials and mission a little easier to evaluate, but people really require getting to know teams. So it is hard.
turns.zh: 所以我喜欢问的问题是：跟我说说你们领导团队上一次战略 offsite。大家在哪意见不合？他们具体在哪一件事上不合？最后在那点上你们站哪边、怎么到的那？我其实让他们告诉我——这像个反向行为面试问题。我让他们告诉我他们怎么 navigate 的，而且我会问 CEO 这个、真的深挖那一组问题。这些是我在评估人的维度时做的，我会说这是最难的一个。财务和使命稍微好评估一点，但人真的需要去了解团队。所以难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a good question to ask. And your point is you can ask that even if you're not a senior leader, you're just ICPM joining a team. Is there anything else you think folks can do? So you said, join some offsites maybe, ask this question that you shared, any other tips for folks just to understand if the people are a good fit? Because it's pretty wild. You're going to spend so much time with these people and you meet them once in a half hour interview and then you have to decide if that's your life for the next four or five, 10 years.
turns.zh: 这问题问得太好了。而且你的点是，就算你不是资深领导、只是个 ICPM 加入团队，也能问这个。还有什么你觉得大家能做的吗？你说，也许参加 offsite、问你分享的这个问题，还有什么建议能帮大家判断人合不合适？因为这挺疯狂的。你要跟这些人花这么多时间，却只在半小时面试里见一次，然后就得决定这是不是你接下来四五年、十年的生活。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Well, one thing that I would say is, you're an investor, right? You invest in a lot of companies, you're an angel investor and you have the Airbnb syndicate and things like that. You evaluate companies when you're making an investment decision, right? Because you're investing a sum of money into that company. And so as a result, you do a lot of diligence on companies or read other people's diligence, something like that. When you're interviewing at a company, you are actually investing an even more scarce resource. You're investing your time. There is no way to get more time. We're all on a finite clock. You can always get more money. If you make a bad investment decision, "Okay, we lost there." Provided you didn't bankrupt yourself. Even if you did, you can climb out of bankruptcy. There are things that you can do, but time is fleeting.
turns.zh: 嗯，我想说的一点是，你是个投资人，对吧？你投很多公司，你是天使投资人，还有 Airbnb 的 syndicate 之类的。你做投资决策时会评估公司，对吧？因为你投了一笔钱进去。所以你会做很多尽调，或者读别人的尽调。你面试一家公司时，你其实在投一种更稀缺的资源。你投的是你的时间。时间没法变多。我们都在有限的钟上。钱你总能再搞到。如果你投资决定做错了，「好，那笔亏了。」只要你没破产。就算破产了，你也能爬出来。有些事你能做，但时间稍纵即逝。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And so one of the other things, and this is a thing that you do when you're an investor, is you do back channel references, right? A company is going to back channel, you the employee, if they're a good company, they're going to talk, if you and I had worked together, Lenny, they might say, "Hey, let me get in touch with Lenny and see what it was really like working with Adam instead of what Adam tells me in the interview process." And you're going to do this as an investor in a company. "Let me talk to some people who passed on investing in this company. What did they see that I don't see?"
turns.zh: 所以另一件你会作为投资人做的事，是做反向背景调查，对吧？一家好公司会对你这个员工做反向调查——他们会去聊，比如你跟我共事过，Lenny，他们可能说「嘿，让我联系下 Lenny，看看跟 Adam 共事真实是什么样，而不是 Adam 在面试里告诉我的」。而你作为公司的投资人也会这么做：「让我跟几个拒绝投资这家公司的人聊聊，他们看到了什么我没看到的？」

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: And so in this case, you can talk to current or former employees who are not on the interview circuit. And because they are not on the interview circuit, their role as a salesperson in the process is greatly diminished. And they can, especially if they're not at the company anymore, give you some pretty candid feedback on what it's like to work there. So I'll give you a really good example. That was super impressive. A PM who worked for me at Patreon, who you know Tal Raviv-
turns.zh: 所以在这种情况下，你可以跟不在面试流程里的现任或前任员工聊。因为他们不在面试流程里，他们在这个过程里当销售员的角色就大大减弱了。他们——尤其如果已经不在公司了——能给你相当坦诚的反馈，讲在那工作是什么样。我给你个超棒的例子。有个在 Patreon 给我干的 PM，你认识的 Tal Raviv——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Shout out Tal.
turns.zh: 致敬 Tal。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: Shout out to Tal, who works on this product that we're recording on right now-
turns.zh: 致敬 Tal，他就在我们现在录这期的这个产品上干活——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Shout out Riverside.
turns.zh: 致敬 Riverside。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: ... when he interviewed at Patreon, he asked me for a list of people who I had managed in the past, and he contacted them to talk to them about what it was like to work for me. That was the first time that had actually ever happened in my career. And I was happy to share that with him. And it represented to me a great level of thoughtfulness and insight around him evaluating what he was getting himself into. And he was an ICPM and he asked that of me, who was a VP executive level person at the company.
turns.zh: ……他面试 Patreon 时，问我要一份我过去管过的人的名单，然后联系他们，聊为我工作是什么样。那是我职业生涯里第一次发生这种事。我很高兴把那个给他。这对我来说，代表着他一种极高的周到和洞察——在评估自己要踏入的是什么。而他当时是个 ICPM，却问了我这个公司里的 VP 级高管。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: So you can do that. And if a company says no or a person says no, I think that actually says a bit more about them than anything else. If they're trying to withhold that from you. Because why would you? If I'm a great manager, I'm happy to have you talk to people who I've managed before, even people maybe who I had to let go or something like that, right? I'm confident that those were the right decisions and that those people ended up in a better place and they were taken care of with great care. I would actually make a reference of somebody who I have let go before just so that someone could get a real honest truth of what it was like working with me. So anyways, that's my take on PMF and questions to ask.
turns.zh: 所以你能这么做。如果一家公司或一个人说不行，我觉得那反而比什么都更能说明他们自己。如果他们想对你隐瞒这个。因为为什么要？如果我是个好经理，我很乐意让你跟我以前管过的人聊，哪怕是那些我可能不得不让走的人，对吧？我有信心那些是正确的决定，那些人最后去了更好的地方、被妥善安置。我甚至会拿一个我以前裁过的人当推荐人，就为了让别人能拿到跟我共事的真实真相。总之，这是我对 PMF 和该问的问题的看法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine you have PMF with your current world, so maybe just to close, can you just remind folks what you're up to now and where they can find you online and also how listeners can be useful to you?
turns.zh: 我猜你现在的状态是 PMF 的，所以也许作为收尾，你能提醒下大家你现在在忙什么、网上哪能找到你，还有听众怎么能帮到你？

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: First, thanks for having me on, Lenny. This was super fun. I love talking about this stuff and it was great chatting with you. So thanks again for having me.
turns.zh: 首先，谢谢你请我上，Lenny。这特别好玩。我爱聊这些，跟你聊很棒。所以再次谢谢你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My pleasure.
turns.zh: 我的荣幸。

turns.speaker: Adam Fishman
turns.en: There are a few ways to get in touch with me. You can follow me and communicate with me on Twitter. My Twitter handle is Fishman, F-I-S-H-M-A-N AF. And I do respond to messages provided that they're polite. And you can also find me on LinkedIn. Those are the two platforms I live on most frequently, for better or for worse. And then I now have this newsletter, fishmanafnewsletter.com.
